title: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: take the full from the full, and the full is what's left

segments.voice: Then two weeks of the peace chants, day three. Yesterday, the three shantis: peace within, peace with others, peace with what no one controls. The week ends on a chant that sounds like a math mistake.

Subtract something and you get less. A kid learns that with a plate of cookies and a hungry sibling. This peace chant breaks the rule, and it does it on purpose. It takes the full from the full, and says the full is what's left. Tradition chants it before the Isha Upanishad, and it is very odd arithmetic to say out loud.
screen: `SUBTRACT, AND GET LESS.` → `FULL FROM FULL.` → `ODD ARITHMETIC.`

segments.voice: It's known by its first words, purnam adah. In plain words: that is full. This is full. From the full, the full comes out. Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Then: Om, peace, peace, peace. The same lines open a section of the Brihadaranyaka too. Some readers hear that as Brahman, beyond what the eye sees, and this as the world, or the self, right here. Both are called full. Not a piece broken off; not a copy that's a little less. The schools of Vedanta explain it in their own ways, but they keep the riddle whole. And look where it sits: before study. Before a single word is read, the chant says nothing about the student is lacking, and nothing the student learns has to be taken from somewhere else. Now the week, in one breath. I am this, and why burn along with the body? Not this, not this. Om's three sounds, and a silence two schools hear differently. Honey, where everything feeds everything. Saha navavatu, us both. Three shantis, three rings. And full from full.
screen: `PURNAM ADAH: THAT IS FULL.` · `THIS IS FULL, TOO.` · `NOTHING TAKEN, NOTHING LESS.` · `THE WEEK, IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Count slowly on your fingers the things that are already whole in your life right now: a person, a room, a meal, this breath. Leave out anything you're still waiting for. When you run out of fingers, start again, and let the count be as full as it already is.
The peace chants, and today purnam adah: from the full, the full; take the full away, and the full remains.
Hold this: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad, full from full, and nothing taken. That's the week.

howItsDone: Purnam adah is chanted as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, before and after its study, and it is also widely chanted on its own at the start of prayers and gatherings.

fork.setup: your older cousin worries that helping you study will make her fall behind on her own work. what would purnam adah say?
options: it will cost her; giving always leaves the giver with less.
from the full, the full: what she gives doesn't make her less.
she should help only once she's already far ahead.
fork.reveal: the chant says the full comes from the full and the full remains. it's a riddle about Brahman and the world, and a fair way to think about what teaching takes.

chat.says: second sunday done. gave the kids everything i had. why do i feel so empty now? 😭
options: full from full, and the full remains: giving it away didn't make you less.
that's the cost of teaching: you give it away, so rest until it refills.
you gave too much; a good teacher keeps some back for herself.
chat.meaning: Purnam adah says the full comes from the full and the full remains. What's given in teaching isn't taken away from the teacher.
